items.title: RAID log
items.tagline: Risks, Assumptions, Issues, Dependencies in one living list.
items.purpose: One page that holds everything that could, does or might block the project. It stops items living in people's heads and email.
items.when: Start in week one. Review it in every weekly meeting and before every steering committee.

columns.label: Action
columns.hint: The next step, not a wish

example.desc: The vendor assistant may not meet the response quality target by pilot (illustrative)
example.action: Agree an evaluation set and a pass mark with the vendor

example.desc: Test environment will have realistic data from week 3
Penetration test report not yet received, so security approval is blocked
example.action: Agree a date with the testing firm and tell the sponsor

example.desc: Single sign-on integration needs the identity team's release in week 5

tips: Give every item one owner, not a team.
Write actions you can tick off, with a date.
Close items properly and keep them for lessons learned.
Review in every weekly meeting or it becomes a graveyard.
mistakes: Listing risks with no owner or action.
Mixing issues (already happening) with risks (might happen).
Updating it only before steering committees.

items.title: Risk register
items.tagline: Score risks so you can decide what to do first.
items.purpose: Goes deeper than the RAID log: it describes each risk, scores it and records the planned response, so effort goes to the biggest risks.
items.when: Create it at planning, review monthly or at each phase, and whenever something big changes.

columns.label: Risk
columns.hint: Because of (cause), (event) may happen, leading to (effect)

columns.label: Score
columns.hint: Likelihood x Impact, calculated for you

columns.label: Trigger
columns.hint: The early sign it is happening

example.risk: Because test data is not realistic, user testing may miss defects, leading to problems after go-live (illustrative)
example.action: Create masked production-like data set, Marcus, by week 3
example.trigger: Testers report data does not match real cases

example.risk: Because the vendor depends on one engineer, a resignation may stop delivery (illustrative)
example.action: Ask for a named deputy and documented handover, Victoria, this month
example.trigger: Vendor changes the team without notice

example.risk: Because the AI assistant may answer from outdated documents, customers may get wrong information (illustrative)
example.action: Name content owners and a monthly review, Daniel, before pilot
example.trigger: Evaluation questions fail on policy topics

tips: Write the cause, the event and the effect, not a vague worry.
Agree what 1 to 5 means so scores are comparable.
Rank by score and attend to the top five.
Record the trigger so you notice early.
mistakes: Scoring everything 3.
Treating the register as a one-time document.
No owner for the response.

items.title: Project charter
items.tagline: A one to two page agreement on why, what, who and how much.
items.purpose: The charter is the sponsor's authority for the project and the reference everyone returns to when scope is argued.
items.when: Before the project starts, signed by the sponsor. Revisit only through change control.

example.content: Let customers track orders online so the contact centre handles fewer routine calls (illustrative).
Portal live for all customers by the agreed date, with the assistant answering approved order questions and a measurable drop in routine calls.
Customer portal, order tracking, AI assistant for order questions, single sign-on, hypercare.
Changes to the warehouse system, new payment methods, other languages in phase one.
Design approved, test environment ready, security review passed, pilot, go-live.
Approved envelope, contingency held by the sponsor (figures to be agreed).
Sponsor Daniel Okafor, PM, business analyst, security lead, operations, vendor.
Fixed contract date, vendor platform used, security gates mandatory.
Vendor quality, data readiness, security approval timing.
Sponsor name, date, signature.

tips: Keep it short enough that people read it.
Write scope out as clearly as scope in.
Get a real signature, not a nod in a meeting.
mistakes: A charter that reads like a plan.
No scope out, so everything is arguable.
Written without the sponsor.

items.title: RACI matrix
items.tagline: Who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
items.purpose: Makes ownership explicit. R does the work, A answers for the result (one person only), C is asked, I is told.
items.when: When roles are unclear, a new team starts, or decisions stall.
tips: Exactly one A on each row.
Too many Rs on a row means unclear ownership.
Use real names in a second version when roles are agreed.
mistakes: Two As on one activity.
Everyone is Consulted on everything.
Never shared with the people in it.

items.title: Business case
items.tagline: The reasons, options and numbers behind the decision to proceed.
items.purpose: Lets a decision maker compare doing nothing, a cheaper option and the recommended option on cost, benefit and risk.
items.when: Before funding is approved and again at stage gates, because benefits and costs change.

example.content: Customers phone the contact centre for routine order status, which is slow for them and costly for us (illustrative).
1 Do nothing. 2 Improve the existing website. 3 New portal with an AI assistant.
Option 3, delivered in phases with a limited pilot first.
Build, vendor licences, run costs including AI usage, training, support (figures to be agreed).
Fewer routine calls, faster answers for customers, better data on questions asked. State how each is measured and who owns it.
Vendor quality, data readiness, adoption.
Pilot, staged release, full release.
Approve Option 3 and the phase one budget by the steering committee date.

tips: Always include a do nothing option.
Give every benefit an owner and a way to measure it.
Show ranges when numbers are uncertain.
mistakes: Benefits nobody owns.
Costs that omit running the service.
A case written to justify a decision already made.

items.title: Test strategy
items.tagline: How you will prove it works before customers find out.
items.purpose: Agrees what will be tested, by whom, in which environment and what counts as good enough to go live.
items.when: During planning, agreed with the business, security and operations before testing starts.

example.content: Show the portal and assistant work for the main customer journeys and are safe to release.
Order tracking, login, assistant answers on approved topics, security checks. Out: warehouse system internals.
Unit and integration by developers, system testing by the test team, user acceptance by the business, security and performance testing.
Dedicated test environment with masked, realistic data. Refresh before each test cycle.
Entry: build deployed and smoke test passed. Exit: no open critical defects, agreed pass mark on the assistant evaluation set, security sign-off.
Severity levels, owners, daily triage, agreed fix times.
Test lead, business testers, developers, security, product owner.
Weekly test progress and defect trend in the status report.

tips: Agree exit criteria with the business before testing starts.
For AI features, include an evaluation set and safety tests.
Plan test data early. It is usually the bottleneck.
mistakes: Testing squeezed at the end.
Exit criteria invented on go-live day.
No test environment owner.

items.title: Status report
items.tagline: One page a busy executive reads in ten seconds.
items.purpose: Shows where the project is, what changed, what is at risk and what you need from the reader.
items.when: Weekly or fortnightly, in the same format each time.

example.content: Amber: security report is late, other work on track.
Test environment ready, single sign-on built, vendor demo completed.
Start user testing, receive penetration test report, agree the pilot group.
Security approval timing (issue), assistant quality (risk). Each with owner and next step.
Sponsor to confirm the pilot customers by Friday.
Spend on plan. Go-live date holds if the report arrives by next Friday.

tips: Put the decision you need at the top, not the bottom.
Use the same layout every time.
Say what changed, not everything that happened.
mistakes: Green until suddenly red.
A page of activity with no decision requested.
Hiding bad news until it is bigger.

items.title: Stakeholder register
items.tagline: Who matters, what they need and how you will keep them with you.
items.purpose: Lists the people who can affect or are affected by the project, with a plan for how to engage each one.
items.when: At the start, and again whenever the team or the politics change.

example.need: Short honest status and early warning

example.interest: No go-live without evidence of safety
example.need: Early sight of the test plan and findings
Training and a clear support route

tips: Be honest about support today. Nobody else reads this.
Plan for the people who can say no, not only your fans.
Revisit after each phase.
mistakes: Sharing the register widely.
Only listing friendly people.
Never updating it.
